question: A 24-year-old sexually active woman presents with a 5-day history of profuse, fishy-smelling, grey-white vaginal discharge. Wet mount shows clue cells; the whiff test is positive with 10% KOH. What is the most likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Candida typically causes thick, white, cottage-cheese-like discharge with intense pruritus and a negative whiff test. Clue cells are not seen in candidiasis.

Correct. The Amsel criteria for bacterial vaginosis require ≥3 of: (1) homogeneous grey-white discharge, (2) pH >4.5, (3) positive whiff test (amine odour with KOH), and (4) clue cells on wet mount. This case fulfils criteria 1, 3, and 4.

Incorrect. Trichomonas causes yellow-green frothy discharge with strawberry cervix; motile trichomonads (not clue cells) are seen on wet mount. Clue cells are characteristic of bacterial vaginosis, not trichomoniasis.
Incorrect. Chlamydia typically causes mucopurulent cervical discharge rather than the homogeneous vaginal grey-white discharge described; clue cells are not a feature of chlamydial infection.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the Amsel criteria for bacterial vaginosis (≥3 of 4: characteristic discharge, pH >4.5, positive whiff test, clue cells on wet mount) and contrast with Candida (pruritus, cottage-cheese, no clue cells) and Trichomonas (frothy yellow-green, motile organisms).
Correct. Clue cells + positive whiff test + grey-white homogeneous discharge = bacterial vaginosis by Amsel criteria. First-line treatment is oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days.
